claims.claim: Sea lions live along the west coast of North America.
claims.quote: California sea lions are “eared seals” native to the West Coast of North America.

claims.claim: They swim in the sea and rest on beaches and docks.
claims.quote: They live in coastal waters and on beaches, docks, buoys, and jetties.

claims.claim: Grown males bark like dogs.
claims.quote: California sea lion males bark like dogs to communicate with other males and females.

claims.claim: California sea lions are eared seals from the West Coast of North America.
claims.quote: California sea lions are “eared seals” native to the West Coast of North America.

claims.claim: They range from southeast Alaska to central Mexico.
claims.quote: California sea lions range from southeast Alaska to the Pacific coast of central Mexico.

claims.claim: They live in shallow coastal water.
claims.quote: California sea lions live in the shallow waters of the eastern North Pacific Ocean.

claims.claim: They rest on beaches, docks, buoys and jetties.
claims.quote: They live in coastal waters and on beaches, docks, buoys, and jetties.

claims.claim: They are playful, clever and very noisy, and sound like barking dogs.
claims.quote: California sea lions are playful, intelligent, and very vocal (sounding like barking dogs).

claims.claim: Grown males are mostly dark brown.
claims.quote: Adult males are generally larger than females and are mostly dark brown to black in color.

claims.claim: Grown males have a raised bump on top of the head.
claims.quote: Mature adult males have a raised forehead called the sagittal crest which increases to about an inch and a half at ten years of age.

claims.claim: Sea lions have small ear flaps you can see.
claims.quote: The species has visible ear pinnae (ear flaps) on either side of its head

claims.claim: True seals have ear holes but no ear flaps.
claims.quote: belong to a group of pinnipeds that have ear holes but lack an external ear flap

claims.claim: Ear flaps are how you tell a sea lion from a true seal.
claims.quote: Their visible ear flaps distinguish them from true seals.

claims.claim: Sea lions are called eared seals because of their external ear flaps.
claims.quote: belong to a group of pinnipeds that have external ear flaps—giving them the nickname “eared seals.”

claims.claim: True seals have ear holes but no outer flap.
claims.quote: belong to a group of pinnipeds that have ear holes but lack an external ear flap

claims.claim: The flaps are small, but sea lions hear well above and below water.
claims.quote: Though the sea lion's ear flaps are small, it can hear quite well both above and below the surface.

claims.claim: Their ears close under water.
claims.quote: Its ears are also valvular and close underwater.

claims.claim: Grown males have a high bump on top of the head, called a crest.
claims.quote: At about 5 years old, males develop a noticeable crest that runs lengthwise along the top of their skull creating a high, domed forehead.

claims.claim: The hair on the crest often turns light.
claims.quote: Subadult and adult males have pronounced forehead crests crowned with tufts of blonde or lighter hair.

claims.claim: Females have no big crest.
claims.quote: Females lack a pronounced crest and have a thinner head that slopes more gently to the end of the muzzle.

claims.claim: As a male grows up, a crest grows along the top of his skull, giving a high, domed forehead.
claims.quote: At about 5 years old, males develop a noticeable crest that runs lengthwise along the top of their skull creating a high, domed forehead.

claims.claim: The crest is a bony bump on top of the skull.
claims.quote: starting at 4 years old, males develop a bony bump on top of their skull known as a sagittal crest, which is fully developed by 7 years old.

claims.claim: On most males the crest gets lighter with age.
claims.quote: On most males, especially darker individuals, the crest and a corresponding area on the muzzle and around the eyes lighten with age.

claims.claim: Females have a thinner head that slopes gently down to the muzzle.
claims.quote: Females lack a pronounced crest and have a thinner head that slopes more gently to the end of the muzzle.

claims.claim: Males are much bigger than females.
claims.quote: Adult males are substantially more robust and larger than females.

claims.claim: The body is smooth and shaped like a torpedo.
claims.quote: They have strong, bulky shoulders and their streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies taper to the tail.

claims.claim: It is big at the shoulders and thin at the tail.
claims.quote: They have strong, bulky shoulders and their streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies taper to the tail.

claims.claim: A layer of blubber keeps it warm.
claims.quote: The blubber layer insulates the California sea lion and streamlines the body.

claims.claim: A sea lion has a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body with strong, bulky shoulders that tapers to the tail.
claims.quote: They have strong, bulky shoulders and their streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies taper to the tail.

claims.claim: A thick layer of blubber lies under the skin.
claims.quote: California sea lions deposit most of their body fat into a thick layer of blubber just under the skin.

claims.claim: Blubber keeps the body warm and streamlined.
claims.quote: The blubber layer insulates the California sea lion and streamlines the body.

claims.claim: Grown males are mostly dark brown.
claims.quote: Adult males are generally larger than females and are mostly dark brown to black in color.

claims.claim: Females and young sea lions are blonde to tan.
claims.quote: Adult females and juveniles are slender-bodied and are blonde to tan in color.

claims.claim: Sea lions swim with their long front flippers.
claims.quote: Their front flippers are especially long and are used for propelling them through the water.

claims.claim: They beat them up and down like wings.
claims.quote: Sea lions swim with up-and-down, wing-like strokes of their foreflippers.

claims.claim: True seals swim with their back flippers instead.
claims.quote: They also use their fore flippers to propel themselves through the water, whereas true seals rely primarily on their back flippers to swim.

claims.claim: The front flippers are long and shaped like wings.
claims.quote: A California sea lions fore flippers are large and winglike, with the skeletal structure of a land animal.

claims.claim: The flippers are dark.
claims.quote: All ages and sexes have contrasting black flippers, naked except for a short stubble of dark fur partially covering the upper surface.

claims.claim: Sea lions swim with up and down strokes of their front flippers.
claims.quote: Sea lions swim with up-and-down, wing-like strokes of their foreflippers.

claims.claim: They paddle with the front flippers and steer with the back flippers.
claims.quote: In the water, they propel themselves by paddling their front flippers and use their rear flippers to help steer, like a boat’s rudder.

claims.claim: True seals swim by moving their back flippers back and forth, like a fish uses its tail.
claims.quote: In the water, seals swim easily, moving their rear flippers back and forth, similar to how a fish uses its caudal fin (tail) to propel itself through the water.

claims.claim: In water the back flippers help steer, like a boat's rudder.
claims.quote: In the water, they propel themselves by paddling their front flippers and use their rear flippers to help steer, like a boat’s rudder.

claims.claim: On land he turns them under his body and walks on all four flippers.
claims.quote: On land, these sea lions move by rotating their rear flippers under their bodies and supporting their body weight on all four flippers.

claims.claim: In the sea the back flippers help steer, like a boat's rudder.
claims.quote: In the water, they propel themselves by paddling their front flippers and use their rear flippers to help steer, like a boat’s rudder.

claims.claim: On land a sea lion turns its back flippers under its body and walks on all four flippers.
claims.quote: On land, these sea lions move by rotating their rear flippers under their bodies and supporting their body weight on all four flippers.

claims.claim: True seals move on land on their bellies, like a caterpillar.
claims.quote: On land, seals use their bellies to move around in a caterpillar-like motion.

claims.claim: The back flippers have claws used for grooming.
claims.quote: Their back flippers are used as rudders and have three claws for grooming.

claims.claim: A grown male is about 2.3 metres (7.5 feet) long.
claims.quote: 6 feet (females) to 7.5 feet (males)

claims.claim: Females are smaller, about 1.8 metres (6 feet).
claims.quote: 6 feet (females) to 7.5 feet (males)

claims.claim: Females grow to about 6 feet and 240 pounds.
claims.quote: 6 feet (females) to 7.5 feet (males)

claims.claim: Other sources give a little more or less.
claims.quote: male sea lions are much larger—reaching up to 600 to 850 pounds and 7 feet in length. Females grow to 200 to 250 pounds and up to 6 feet in length.

claims.claim: A newborn pup is about 75 centimetres long.
claims.quote: Pups are about 2.5 feet (75 centimeters) long, nose to tail tip, and weigh about 18 pounds (8 kilograms) at birth.

claims.claim: A newborn pup weighs 13 to 20 pounds.
claims.quote: Newborn California sea lions weigh 13 to 20 pounds

claims.claim: Sea lions jump out of the water as they swim; this is called porpoising.
claims.quote: They are sometimes seen porpoising, or jumping out of the water, presumably to speed up their swimming.

claims.claim: It may help them swim faster.

claims.claim: Its whiskers feel fish moving nearby, even in the dark.
claims.quote: Their sensitive whiskers, called vibrissae, can rotate forward and detect the slight movements of fish swimming nearby, enabling California sea lions to find and capture prey in total darkness.

claims.claim: Sea lions have good eyes for dim water.
claims.quote: Their eyesight is well developed, because they spend a lot of time underwater with reduced light levels.

claims.claim: In total darkness their whiskers can turn forward and feel the movements of nearby fish.
